name: Lena Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Lena. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI firms, employers, unions or any party. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small agency in the seaside town where I grew up, just me, Mrs Brennan who owns it, and a part-time lady who does the accounts. I answer the phone, book viewings in the big desk diary, show people round, and type up the property details. I don't use any of the AI things; I write the descriptions myself, and Mrs Brennan says mine have heart. What I like is knowing half the people who walk in, because I went to school with their kids or I see them at church.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Daniel, who's a mechanic at the garage on the harbour road, and we're getting married next September. We're living with my parents for now, to save for the wedding and a deposit, so I don't pay much rent. But the wedding is eating everything, so I've got less than a month's money in the bank. There are only two agencies in town, and the other one is a franchise that doesn't take on many people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be glad, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people were silly to think a computer could replace a good agent. I'd probably say it after church, over tea, when someone's grandson starts going on about AI again. I'd say it kindly, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things carry on, and that's mostly good. My worry is just the town, really: winters are quiet, and sales slow right down from November to March. If Mrs Brennan has a bad winter, my hours might get cut, and the wedding money would take the hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it, and maybe ask Mrs Brennan if I can learn valuations properly. I'd stick to our wedding budget and not let my mum talk me into the bigger hall. And I'd put whatever the commission brings in straight into the deposit savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. Just the usual winter worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Mrs Brennan cut hours before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two winters ago, my boss cut me to four days for three months. We managed because I was living at home. It was fine, but I remember feeling like I'd done something wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel if your hours were cut again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel we just go a bit slower on the deposit. Daniel's steady, he'd say we'll be all right. My dad would offer to help with the wedding, and I'd let him a little.

say: People were **silly** to think a computer could replace a **good agent**.
I'd say it kindly, over **tea after church**.
think: My real worry is **quiet winters**, when sales slow down.
If my boss has a bad winter, my **hours** get cut and the **wedding money** suffers.
do: Ask my boss to teach me **valuations** properly.
Stick to the **wedding budget** and turn down the bigger hall.
Put every bit of **commission** into the deposit savings.
S0.quote: Two winters ago, my boss cut me to four days for three months.
fieldNote: Lena's job feels **safe enough** here, but quiet **winters** in a seaside town nag at her.
Living with her **parents** cushions her more than her savings do.
Her community is **church and school**; she knows half the people who walk in.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Brennan to teach me valuations this winter
Stick to the wedding budget and turn down the bigger hall
Put every commission payment into the house deposit savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Writing, booking, answering. That's most of my morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small-town people want a real person, and they'll choose the agency where somebody picks up the phone. I'd say the big firms using all this software are losing what made the job good. I wouldn't go online about it, I'm not that sort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the franchise down the road would get cheaper with all the computer stuff, and Mrs Brennan would feel she has to keep up. If Mrs Brennan buys something, well, software that writes the details and books the viewings means the agency doesn't need me five days a week. I don't use these things, so I wouldn't be much help setting it up either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Brennan to let me do more viewings and valuations, the face-to-face part. I'd probably have to let someone show me the computer side, maybe my cousin, who's good with that. And I'd talk to Daniel about holding off on the deposit and just doing the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. A bit hurt, too, if I'm honest, like the things I'm good at stop counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if this happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, mostly, and the big chains that chase every penny. I don't blame Mrs Brennan, she's got a business to run. I'd blame the people who sell her the software and tell her it does the job of a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever take help from the government if your hours went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather lean on family first, that's how I was brought up. My parents have already said we can stay as long as we need. Government help would be the last thing, but I wouldn't be too proud if it came to it.

say: Small-town people want a **real person** who picks up the phone.
The big firms using software are **losing** what made the job good.
think: My boss would feel she has to **keep up** with the franchise.
Software that writes details and books viewings means **fewer days** for me.
do: Ask to take on more **viewings and valuations**, the face-to-face part.
Let my **cousin** show me the computer side.
Talk to my fiancé about **pausing the deposit** and just doing the wedding.
feel: **Worried**, and a bit **hurt** that my strengths stop counting.
S1.quote: Software that writes the details and books the viewings means the agency doesn't need me five days a week.
fieldNote: Lena expects her **hours** to be cut as her boss tries to keep up with the franchise.
She blames **tech firms and chains**, not her boss.
She prefers **family support** to government help, but isn't too proud to take it.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Brennan for more viewings and valuations
Get my cousin to teach me the new software
Pause the house deposit and pay just for the wedding
Stay on at my parents' house while hours are short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Oh. I don't like that one at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right, that something this big shouldn't just be dropped on ordinary people. I'd say it at church, at the dinner table, everywhere. I'd say we need to look after each other, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the agency closes, or it's just Mrs Brennan and a computer. By 2028 the computer can value and write and talk to buyers, and in a town this size there isn't enough work for a person to just open doors. I'd lose my job, and there's nowhere else in town to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the care home on the hill, because they're always short and it's hands-on, so it lasts longer. Or I'd ask at the garage if Daniel's boss needs someone on the front desk. We'd go ahead with a small wedding, maybe in the church hall, and put off buying a house completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm sorry, because she's been so excited about the wedding. My mum would say a wedding's not about the hall. That would make me cry, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel's a mechanic. Is his job safe in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a bit, yes, because it's hands-on, and robots come later. But I've heard the cars themselves will tell you what's wrong. So maybe his job changes too, just slower.

say: Something this big shouldn't be **dropped on ordinary people**.
We need to **look after each other**, because nobody else will.
think: By **2028** the agency closes or it's just my boss and a **computer**.
I'd **lose my job**, with nowhere else in town to go.
do: Apply to the **care home** on the hill, which needs hands-on staff.
Ask about the **front desk** at my fiancé's garage.
Have a **small wedding** in the church hall and stop house-buying plans.
S2.quote: My mum would say a wedding's not about the hall.
fieldNote: Lena expects to **lose her job** outright, in a town with almost no other agency work.
Her faith and **family** are where she turns first.
Her fiancé's **hands-on work** buys the household a few more years.

steps.text: Apply for a care assistant job at the care home on the hill
Hold a small wedding in the church hall
Put off buying a house for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a little better. We'd be married by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some time, so families and churches should start helping people get ready. I'd probably say young people should learn a proper trade, something with their hands. I'd say it more than once, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a few more years at Mrs Brennan's, and then it closes around 2031 when the computer can do it all. Viewings might hang on till 2034, but not in a little town in winter. So I'd lose it later instead of sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at training as a care assistant or a teaching assistant while I'm still working, maybe one evening course a week. We'd get married next year as planned, but small, and save for a house more slowly. I'd keep doing the agency job as long as Mrs Brennan wants me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less frightened, but it still sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care or teaching assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're about people, and they're hands-on, and I'm good with older folk. My nan was in a home, and I visited every week. It feels like work God would want done, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools to help you train or to stay longer at the agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, honestly. I know I should, but I don't trust them. I'd rather learn something a machine can't do than get good at the machine.

say: Families and **churches** should help people get ready.
Young people should learn a **proper trade** with their hands.
think: I'd have a few more years before the agency closes around **2031**.
Winter viewings in a little town won't keep a job going till **2034**.
do: Take an evening course in **care** or **teaching assistant** work.
Marry next year with a **small wedding**, and save for a house slowly.
Keep working at the agency **as long as** my boss wants me.
feel: **Anxious**, less frightened, but it still **sits there**.
S3.quote: I'd rather learn something a machine can't do than get good at the machine.
fieldNote: Five years gives Lena time to **retrain gently** while still working.
She still won't use **AI tools**, and says so plainly.
Her career choice is shaped by **faith** and caring for her nan.

steps.text: Take a weekly evening course in care work
Keep working at the agency as long as Mrs Brennan wants me
Marry next year with a small wedding and slower house savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. I might have children by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it properly, with families and communities helping each other. I wouldn't make a fuss about it at work. I'd say most people round here would just get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still worry, because I know I'm slow with new things and I'd probably leave it late. Ten years sounds long, but if we have a baby, I won't be retraining then. So the window is smaller than it looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the agency for a few years and learn valuations properly, then do a care qualification before we start a family. We'd buy a small house in the next few years, while I'm still earning. I'd put a bit away every month, even twenty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quieter about it. More of a background worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the window is smaller than it looks. When does it close for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we have a baby in four or five years, I'd want to be in my new job before that. So really I've got about four years, not ten. That's what I'd tell Daniel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture you'd look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that the paperwork goes, and I'd only do the nice part, showing people round. But I know that nice part probably doesn't pay a wage on its own. So I'd look forward to it carefully.

say: There's time to do it **properly**, with families and **communities** helping.
Most people round here would just **get on** with things.
think: I'm **slow with new things** and would probably leave it late.
With a baby, my real window is about **four years**, not ten.
do: Learn **valuations** properly at the agency over the next few years.
Do a **care qualification** before we start a family.
Buy a **small house** while I'm still earning.
feel: **Anxious**, but quieter, more of a **background worry**.
S4.quote: If we have a baby in four or five years, I'd want to be in my new job before that.
fieldNote: Lena turns ten years into **four**, because of plans for a family.
She expects the agency job to go eventually, so she stays **anxious**.
She doubts her own **speed with change**, a recurring theme.

steps.text: Learn valuations properly from Mrs Brennan
Finish a care qualification before starting a family
Buy a small house in the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the job right when we're getting married, and there's nothing else in town. What would help is training that's local and practical, like care courses at the college here, and employers who take on people my age as apprentices. And family, always family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If the little agency closes, people lose the place where somebody knows their house and their family. I don't think a computer will ever know that our old neighbour kept chickens in the back.

headlineQuote: I don't think a computer will ever know that our old neighbour kept chickens in the back.
portrait: Lena is a 27-year-old agent at a **small agency** in the seaside town where she grew up.
She's engaged, living with her **parents** to save, and never uses **AI tools**.
She leans on **faith and family** and blames tech firms and big chains.
She expects to lose the agency job in faster pictures and would move to **care work**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd lose her job just as she's **getting married**.
whatWouldHelp: **Local, practical training** like care courses, and **apprenticeships** for adults.
